passage: On the balcony of their Chennai flat, Devika blew through a bubble wand. Manjula, two, gasped and clapped her hands, mouth wide in a round "oh." A bubble landed on her nose and popped; she squealed and blinked. "More?" said Devika. Manjula nodded hard and stretched her arms. The moment passed quickly, and Devika blew again, so it returned, and Manjula stayed against her leg, laughing.

qa.q: Where did Devika blow bubbles?
qa.a: Devika blew them on the balcony of their flat.

qa.q: What does Manjula's round oh and clapping suggest, and what else might explain her blink?
qa.a: They suggest pleased surprise at the bubbles. The blink probably came from the bubble popping on her nose, not from unhappiness.

qa.q: Why does Devika blow again?
qa.a: Repeating the fun lets Manjula feel safe delight in something she now knows will happen. 😊

qa.q: How might Devika feel watching Manjula?
qa.a: Devika probably feels tender and amused, enjoying Manjula's joy.

grounding: A toddler gasps and claps at bubbles, and repeating the fun lets the child feel safe delight.

passage:
"Where did the ball go?" said Raghav, covering the red ball with a cup.
"Ball!" said Hemant.
"Gone! Under the cup. One, two..." He lifted the cup. "Boo!"
Hemant gasped and clapped. "Again!"
Raghav did it again, then with a hat.
"Ball!" Hemant shrieked and clapped, leaning in until his nose almost touched the hat.

qa.q: What did Raghav hide the ball under first?
qa.a: He hid it under a cup.

qa.q: What does Hemant's gasp and clap suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests pleased surprise at the ball appearing. It could also be excitement at Raghav's playful voice.

qa.q: What could Raghav do to keep the game working?
qa.a: He can keep the surprise gentle and the pattern familiar, and change small things like the hat.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel if a stranger did the game suddenly?
qa.a: He might feel startled instead of delighted, since the trust with Raghav is part of the fun.

grounding: A toddler gasps and claps at a surprise game, and repeating the fun lets him feel safe delight.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. When I blew bubbles in the garden today, Madhav gasped, his mouth making a big "O", and clapped fast. The bubbles popped and his clapping stopped just as quickly. I blew more. Same gasp, same clap, every time. We did it maybe fifteen times, and he never got tired of it. Wasim, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Madhav do when he saw the bubbles?
qa.a: He gasped, his mouth making a big "O", and clapped fast.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling each time the bubbles appeared?
qa.a: He felt a burst of delighted surprise, which faded quickly and returned each time.

qa.q: Why was repeating the bubbles a good idea?
qa.a: Because repeating the surprise let Madhav enjoy the same safe delight again and again.

qa.q: How might Madhav's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably smile and feel happy to picture his joy.

grounding: A teacher repeats bubbles for a toddler who gasps and claps in delighted surprise each time.

passage:
At the temple fair in their small town, Parveen bought a paper pinwheel and held it up in the wind. It began to spin. Shankar, on her hip, gasped and clapped, then reached for it.
Parveen blew on it. It spun faster. Shankar gasped again, just as big, and clapped harder.
"Again?" asked his aunt. She blew, and he squealed.

qa.q: What did Parveen buy at the fair?
qa.a: A paper pinwheel.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when the pinwheel spun?
qa.a: He was delighted and surprised, gasping and clapping each time.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that helped Shankar enjoy it?
qa.a: She repeated the spin by blowing, so he could feel the safe delight again.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel seeing Shankar squeal?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and pleased with her small purchase. 🎉

grounding: A toddler gasps and claps at a spinning pinwheel, and his aunt repeats the fun.

passage:
In their Hamburg kitchen, Felix set a toy car at the top of a cardboard ramp and let go. It zoomed down and shot across the floor.
Yara gasped, hands flying up, and then clapped. "Again!"
Felix set it up again. Zoom. Gasp. Clap.
By the sixth time, she was clapping before the car even reached the bottom, laughing.

qa.q: What did Felix build for the car?
qa.a: A cardboard ramp.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling as she began clapping before the car reached the bottom?
qa.a: She was delighted and excited, now expecting the fun surprise because it was repeated.

qa.q: What made Felix's game work well for Yara?
qa.a: He repeated the same surprise, so she could feel safe delight and anticipation.

qa.q: How might Felix feel after the sixth run?
qa.a: He probably feels amused and pleased to see her enjoyment grow.

grounding: A toddler gasps and claps at a toy car's surprise run, and repeating it lets her enjoy safe delight.

passage:
I'm Nazia. My little brother Asif had never seen bubbles before last week.
I blew the first one and it floated right past his nose. He gasped, eyes wide, and clapped his hands together, fast.
Then it popped, and he looked at me, mouth open.
So I blew another. Gasp, clap. Another. Gasp, clap, and this time a squeal.
We did it about twenty times. He never got bored.

qa.q: About how many times did Nazia blow bubbles?
qa.a: About twenty times.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he gasped and clapped at the bubble?
qa.a: He was surprised and delighted, a quick burst of pleased excitement at something new.

qa.q: Why was blowing the bubbles again and again a good idea?
qa.a: Repeating the fun let Asif enjoy the surprise safely, knowing another bubble would come.

qa.q: What would change if Nazia had blown only one bubble?
qa.a: Asif might have been left puzzled and disappointed when it popped, without the chance to enjoy the surprise again.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler gasping and clapping at bubbles in pleased surprise, with a sibling repeating the fun.
